adversarial_critique: Claude's coding of S593 as 'Mixed' (with `outcome_family = primary_connection` and `ai_scope_check = passed`) is substantively unsupported and suffers from four compounding methodological and metadata defects. First, the dependent variable in all 18 Tobit regressions (Tables 9–14, PDF pp. 10–12) and 18 OLS regressions (Table 15, PDF p. 15) is neither household water connection (`primary_connection`) nor household tariff affordability, but each municipality's component of Coulter's coefficient of distributional inequity comparing Xi/sum(Xi) against population share Ei. Second, as demonstrated in Table 7 (PDF p. 7), page 8, and Footnote 14 (PDF pp. 8–9), applying Coulter's population-share formula to non-additive rates and prices (water supply rate %, unit price won/m3, cost recovery %) sets Xi/S near 1/152 (~0.66%) for every jurisdiction and therefore mechanically scores populous, fiscally independent cities with ~98–100% piped coverage and low tariffs (405–629 won/m3) as 'highly inequitable', leading the author to prescribe massive urban tariff hikes (e.g., +5,105 won/m3 in Gb 01). Third, Claude's structured SWiM row inverts `outcome_polarity` as 'higher = better' even though Coulter's inequity index is scaled 0 = perfect equity to 100 = extreme inequity (higher = worse), creating an internal sign-polarity contradiction with `estimate_short` (-0.917). Fourth, `exposure_short` ('Si (urban) district status' vs. 'gun (rural) districts') is uniformly negative across all 18 models (significant in 15/18, null in customer satisfaction Table 14), so 'Mixed' is obtained only by bundling `si/gun` with two general municipal fiscal variables (`Degree of financial independence` > 0 and `Local tax burden per person` < 0) while ignoring that both actual water-utility governance controls—`Private consignment` (delegated operation, e.g., K-water) and `Local public enterprise status` (corporatized special account)—are statistically null across 35 of 36 Tobit cells (Tables 9–14).

numerical_check_note: All seven stored 2021 Tobit point estimates and N = 152 match Tables 9–14 (PDF pp. 10–12) verbatim to four decimal places: Administrative district unit (si=1) on average unit price = -0.9174 (SE 0.3006, p<0.01, Table 9; -0.917 in OLS Table 15), cost-recovery rate = -0.9064 (SE 0.3714, p<0.05, Table 10), revenue-water ratio = -0.8489 (SE 0.3290, p<0.05, Table 11), water-supply rate = -0.8566 (SE 0.3149, p<0.01, Table 12), and number of employees = -1.1569 (SE 0.3726, p<0.01, Table 13), with customer satisfaction null (-0.2666, SE 0.3579, Table 14); 2021 average unit price coefficients for Degree of financial independence (0.1353, SE 0.0141, p<0.01) and Local tax burden per person (-1.9115, SE 0.4815, p<0.01) also match Table 9 exactly. However, two minor numerical inaccuracies appear in the stored text/dossier: (1) `estimate_full` states Local tax burden per person is significant 'on all 6 variables at p<0.01 in all 3 years', whereas in Table 14 (customer satisfaction, PDF p. 12; also OLS Table 15, PDF p. 15) the 2010 (-1.1847**, SE 0.5092) and 2021 (-1.3969**, SE 0.5732) estimates are significant only at p<0.05 (**), as explicitly noted in text on PDF p. 11 ('유의수준 1%, 5% 기준'); and (2) the dossier SE range '0.3006-0.6' rounds the maximum SE of Local tax burden (0.5968 in Table 13) to 0.6 while omitting the much smaller SEs for Degree of financial independence (0.0120–0.0180 across Tables 9–14).
polarity_or_orientation_issue: Three severe polarity/orientation traps occur: (1) Inverted `outcome_polarity` metadata: Claude coded `outcome_polarity = 'higher = better'` by naming `outcome_short` 'equity of unit price and cost recovery', whereas the actual dependent variable in Eq. (1), Table 4, and Tables 9–15 is Coulter's 'Coefficient of inequity' (0 = perfect equity to 100 = extreme inequity; higher = greater inequity / worse equity), so negative coefficients (-0.9174) mean lower Coulter inequity, not worse equity. (2) Exposure-bundling distortion: `exposure_short` ('Si (urban) district status' vs. 'gun (rural) districts') has a consistent negative raw sign across all 18 models (significant in 15/18, null in 3/18), not 'mixed'; Claude obtained 'mixed' only by combining `si/gun` with two continuous fiscal variables (`Degree of financial independence` [+] and `Local tax burden per person` [-]) from the same equation while ignoring null water-governance controls (`Private consignment` and `Local public enterprise status`). (3) Substantive polarity inversion between Coulter inequity and household access/affordability: because Coulter compares non-additive rates/prices (Xi/S ~ 1/152) against municipal population share Ei, lower Coulter 'inequity' does not mean higher water coverage or more affordable tariffs—populous cities with ~98–100% coverage and low tariffs (405–629 won/m3) score as highly 'inequitable' and would have to raise household tariffs up to 5,734 won/m3 to reduce Coulter inequity (Table 7, Footnote 14).
